subject: science
title: KS3 Science diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science programme of study (2013)

skills.name: Biology
skills.why: KS3 biology lays the groundwork for cells, the body and ecosystems at GCSE.
skills.strong: {name} knows cells, the body and food chains well and can explain how they work.
skills.developing: {name} knows the basic facts but is less sure explaining how living things work together.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with the basics of cells and the human body. These ideas return at GCSE, so they are worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will connect the facts into clear explanations, using diagrams and everyday examples.

skills.name: Chemistry
skills.why: KS3 chemistry introduces the particle ideas that all of GCSE chemistry depends on.
skills.strong: {name} understands states of matter, reactions and compounds well.
skills.developing: {name} knows everyday chemistry facts but is less sure about reactions and compounds.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with materials, acids and separating mixtures. These are the building blocks of chemistry, so they come first.
skills.next_step: We will use simple models of particles to make reactions easier to picture.

skills.name: Physics
skills.why: Physics at KS3 is where students first use equations, a skill that carries straight into GCSE.
skills.strong: {name} uses physics ideas and simple equations confidently.
skills.developing: {name} knows the ideas but is less confident using equations such as weight and moments.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with energy, forces and simple equations. Getting these secure now makes GCSE physics much easier.
skills.next_step: We will practise a simple routine for equations: write it down, put the numbers in, check the units.

skills.name: Working scientifically
skills.why: Planning fair tests and reading results is tested in every science topic.
skills.strong: {name} plans fair tests and handles results confidently.
skills.developing: {name} understands fair testing but is less sure describing patterns in results.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with fair tests and measuring. These skills run through every topic, so they are worth securing.
skills.next_step: We will practise planning experiments and reading results together.

questions.stem: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.explain: The heart pumps blood. The lungs exchange gases.

questions.stem: Which of these is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explain: Water is a liquid at room temperature. Iron and salt are solids; oxygen is a gas.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explain: Wind will not run out. Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment measures the volume of a liquid most accurately?
questions.explain: A measuring cylinder has a fine scale. Beaker markings are only approximate.

questions.stem: Which part of a cell controls its activities and contains its genetic material?
questions.explain: The nucleus holds the DNA and controls the cell. The membrane controls what enters and leaves.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a neutral solution, such as pure water?
questions.explain: pH 7 is neutral. Below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline.

questions.stem: A runner travels 100 m in 20 s. What is their average speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s. 2000 multiplies instead.

questions.stem: How do you make an experiment a fair test?
options: Change lots of variables at once
Change only one variable and keep the others the same
questions.explain: Change one variable and control the rest, so any difference is caused by that one change.

questions.stem: Which gas do plants take in from the air to use in photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide. Oxygen is released, not taken in, during photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which method would you use to get solid salt back from salty water?
questions.explain: Evaporate the water and the salt is left behind. Filtration cannot remove a dissolved solid.

questions.stem:
A student measures the temperature of some water three times:
21 °C, 23 °C, 22 °C

What is the mean temperature?
What happens to light when it hits a flat mirror?
questions.explain: Mirrors reflect light. Refraction is bending as light passes between materials.

questions.stem: A student finds that the higher the temperature of the water, the faster sugar dissolves. What type of relationship is this?
questions.explain: As one variable increases, so does the other: a positive relationship (correlation).

questions.stem:
Look at this food chain:
grass → rabbit → fox

If all the foxes were removed, what would most likely happen to the number of rabbits at first?
questions.explain: With no predator, fewer rabbits are eaten, so their numbers rise at first.

questions.stem:
Complete this word equation with the name of the missing gas:
magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + ______
questions.explain: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are common wrong guesses.

questions.stem:
Weight = mass × gravitational field strength
What is the weight of a 5 kg bag on Earth, where the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg?
questions.explain: 5 × 10 = 50 N. 0.5 divides instead.

questions.stem: Why do scientists share their results so that other scientists can check them?
options: So other scientists can check the method and conclusions
So nobody needs to do the experiment again
questions.explain: Peer review lets others check and repeat the work, which makes conclusions more trustworthy.

questions.stem: The inside of the small intestine is covered in millions of tiny, finger-like villi. Explain how the villi help the body.

rubric.criterion: Villi give a large surface area
So digested food can be absorbed into the blood more quickly (or more food is absorbed)

questions.explain: Accept 'more space to absorb food' for the surface area mark. 'They digest food' alone earns nothing.

questions.stem: Which of these is a compound?
questions.explain: A compound contains two or more different elements joined together: carbon and oxygen in CO₂. O₂ and H₂ are molecules of one element.

questions.stem:
A force of 20 N acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment of the force?
Moment = force × distance from the pivot
questions.explain: 20 × 0.5 = 10 N m. 40 divides instead.
